Chapter Two: From Printing Presses to Bicycles—Learning by Doing.
Picture this: two young brothers, full of curiosity, stepping into the world of business and invention. They didn’t start with a grand factory. Instead, they rolled up their sleeves and launched a neighborhood newspaper, using a printing press they built themselves. The work? It was tough. The profits? Pretty modest. But what they gained was priceless—lessons in persistence, problem-solving, and why quality really matters.
Running their print shop meant paying close attention to every detail—there was no one to call when a machine broke down. So, what did they do? They figured it out themselves. Over time, they became skilled mechanics, able to fix almost anything that came their way. This hands-on learning wasn’t just about fixing machines; it was about building confidence and resourcefulness—skills that would shape their future adventures.
Now, the world around them was changing fast. And these brothers? They noticed. The bicycle craze was taking over the country, and they saw an opportunity to turn their mechanical know-how into a real business. So, they opened a small bicycle shop—selling, repairing, and, eventually, building their own bikes from scratch. The work demanded long hours and plenty of sweat, but there was a special kind of pride in crafting something with your own hands. Imagine seeing a customer ride away on a bicycle you built—it’s a feeling that sticks with you.
Most folks thought bicycles were just a trend. But the brothers saw something deeper. They understood the importance of balance, control, and precision—skills that, one day, would be crucial in their quest to fly. They also picked up on the value of listening to customers, staying flexible, and never settling for “just good enough.”
Their shop became more than a business—it turned into a laboratory. A place where ideas could be tested, tweaked, and improved. The brothers experimented with new designs, tried out different materials, and searched for better ways to do things. They devoured every book they could find on mechanics and engineering, often staying up late just to talk through their latest discoveries.
Through all the ups and downs, family was their anchor. Katharine, now a teacher, helped keep everything running smoothly and lifted their spirits when things got tough. Their father, even while traveling for church work, sent them letters filled with advice and encouragement.
Looking back, it’s clear how these years shaped their approach to invention. They learned that real success doesn’t come quickly or easily. There are always setbacks, and the only way forward is through hard work and determination. They discovered the power of working together—of sharing ideas, solving problems, and reaching for goals as a team.
In a world that often puts so much emphasis on degrees and formal training, these brothers showed us something important. Self-education and hands-on experience can be just as powerful. Innovation isn’t reserved only for experts. It’s open to anyone willing to get their hands dirty, take risks, and keep learning.
